summary: This RFC describes using AES in CCM mode within TLS and DTLS to provide confidentiality and data origin authentication. CCM allows compact implementations, which suits constrained environments such as small devices.

plainLanguage.summary: Some small devices have to run TLS but do not have room for a large crypto library. AES-CCM helps them: it encrypts and checks the message in one operation, and it only needs the encrypt direction of the AES cipher, never the decrypt direction. This document defines the TLS cipher suites that use it, including versions with a shorter check tag for networks where every byte counts.

subtitle: Sixteen TLS cipher suites that use AES in CCM mode, built for small devices.

tldr.problem: Small, constrained devices need TLS and DTLS cipher suites that encrypt and authenticate data without much code, because CCM needs only the AES encrypt operation.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC defines 16 cipher suites that use AES-128 or AES-256 in CCM mode as an AEAD algorithm in TLS 1.2, with RSA or pre-shared-key key establishment. Suites ending in _8 use a shorter 8-octet authentication tag instead of 16 octets.
tldr.outcome: They can only be used with TLS 1.2 or later. The RFC is a Proposed Standard and was later updated by RFC 10015.

facts.label: Nonce length
facts.value: 12 bytes: a 4-octet salt and an 8-octet nonce_explicit

facts.label: Authentication tag
facts.value: 16 octets, or 8 octets for the _8 suites

today: RFC 6655 is a Proposed Standard published in July 2012. It has not been obsoleted, but it was updated by RFC 10015.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
This document describes the use of the Advanced Encryption Standard in Counter with CBC-MAC Mode, or CCM, in several TLS ciphersuites. AES-CCM provides both authentication and confidentiality and uses as its only primitive the AES encrypt operation, because the AES decrypt operation is not needed. This makes it amenable to compact implementations, which is advantageous in constrained environments. Adoption outside of constrained environments is necessary to enable interoperability, such as that between web clients and embedded servers or between embedded clients and web servers. The use of AES-CCM has been specified for IPsec Encapsulating Security Payload and for 802.15.4 wireless networks.

Authenticated encryption, in addition to providing confidentiality for the plaintext that is encrypted, provides a way to check its integrity and authenticity. Authenticated Encryption with Associated Data, or AEAD, adds the ability to check the integrity and authenticity of some associated data that is not encrypted. This document uses the AEAD facility within TLS 1.2 and the AES-CCM-based AEAD algorithms defined in RFC 5116. Additional AEAD algorithms are defined that use AES-CCM but have shorter authentication tags and are therefore more suitable for use across networks in which bandwidth is constrained and message sizes may be small.

The ciphersuites defined in this document use RSA or Pre-Shared Key as their key establishment mechanism, and can be used with DTLS. Since the ability to use AEAD ciphers was introduced in DTLS version 1.2, the ciphersuites defined in this document cannot be used with earlier versions of that protocol.
sections.plainLanguage: Some small devices have to run TLS but do not have room for a large crypto library. AES-CCM helps them: it encrypts and checks the message in one operation, and it only needs the encrypt direction of the AES cipher, never the decrypt direction. This document defines the TLS cipher suites that use it, including versions with a shorter check tag for networks where every byte counts.

sections.title: RSA-Based AES-CCM Cipher Suites
sections.content:
The ciphersuites are based on the AES-CCM AEAD algorithms AEAD_AES_128_CCM and AEAD_AES_256_CCM described in RFC 5116. Eight RSA-based ciphersuites are defined: TLS_RSA_WITH_AES_128_CCM at 0xC0,0x9C; TLS_RSA_WITH_AES_256_CCM at 0xC0,0x9D; TLS_DHE_RSA_WITH_AES_128_CCM at 0xC0,0x9E; TLS_DHE_RSA_WITH_AES_256_CCM at 0xC0,0x9F; TLS_RSA_WITH_AES_128_CCM_8 at 0xC0,0xA0; TLS_RSA_WITH_AES_256_CCM_8 at 0xC0,0xA1; TLS_DHE_RSA_WITH_AES_128_CCM_8 at 0xC0,0xA2; and TLS_DHE_RSA_WITH_AES_256_CCM_8 at 0xC0,0xA3.

Each uses AES-CCM; those that end in _8 have an 8-octet authentication tag, while the other ciphersuites have 16-octet authentication tags. The HMAC truncation option described in RFC 6066, which negotiates the truncated_hmac TLS extension, does not have an effect on cipher suites that do not use HMAC.

The nonce input to the AEAD algorithm is exactly that of the AES-GCM cipher suites: it SHALL be 12 bytes long and is constructed from a 4-octet salt and an 8-octet nonce_explicit. The salt is the implicit part of the nonce and is not sent in the packet. Instead, the salt is generated as part of the handshake process: it is either the client_write_IV when the client is sending, or the server_write_IV when the server is sending. The nonce_explicit is the explicit part of the nonce, chosen by the sender and carried in each TLS record in the GenericAEADCipher.nonce_explicit field. Each value of the nonce_explicit MUST be distinct for each distinct invocation of the encrypt function for any fixed key, and failure to meet this uniqueness requirement can significantly degrade security. The nonce_explicit MAY be the 64-bit sequence number, as long as those values are assured to meet the distinctness requirement. In DTLS the 64-bit seq_num is the 16-bit epoch concatenated with the 48-bit seq_num.

These ciphersuites make use of the default TLS 1.2 pseudorandom function, which uses HMAC with the SHA-256 hash function, and the RSA and DHE_RSA key exchange is performed as defined in the TLS 1.2 specification.
sections.plainLanguage: Eight RSA-based suites are defined, in four pairs: one for each combination of key exchange and key size, with a full-length or shortened tag. The nonce is 12 bytes long. Four of those bytes are the salt, which comes from the handshake and never travels in the packet, and eight are the explicit part, which the sender puts in each record and which must never repeat for a given key.

sections.title: PSK-Based AES-CCM Cipher Suites
sections.content:
As in the previous section, these ciphersuites follow RFC 5116, and the PSK and DHE_PSK key exchange is performed as in RFC 4279. Eight PSK-based ciphersuites are defined: TLS_PSK_WITH_AES_128_CCM at 0xC0,0xA4; TLS_PSK_WITH_AES_256_CCM at 0xC0,0xA5; TLS_DHE_PSK_WITH_AES_128_CCM at 0xC0,0xA6; TLS_DHE_PSK_WITH_AES_256_CCM at 0xC0,0xA7; TLS_PSK_WITH_AES_128_CCM_8 at 0xC0,0xA8; TLS_PSK_WITH_AES_256_CCM_8 at 0xC0,0xA9; TLS_PSK_DHE_WITH_AES_128_CCM_8 at 0xC0,0xAA; and TLS_PSK_DHE_WITH_AES_256_CCM_8 at 0xC0,0xAB.

The nonce input to the AEAD algorithm is defined as in the previous section. These ciphersuites make use of the default TLS 1.2 pseudorandom function, which uses HMAC with the SHA-256 hash function, and the PSK and DHE_PSK key exchange is performed as defined in RFC 5487.
sections.plainLanguage: Eight more suites are defined for the pre-shared key key exchange, with the same AEAD algorithms, the same nonce and the same tag lengths as the RSA-based ones. They exist so that a device that already shares a secret with the server can use the same small cipher without any public-key arithmetic.

sections.title: TLS Versions
sections.content: These ciphersuites make use of the authenticated encryption with additional data defined in TLS 1.2. Earlier versions of TLS do not have support for AEAD; for instance, the TLSCiphertext structure does not have the aead option in TLS 1.1. Consequently, these ciphersuites MUST NOT be negotiated in older versions of TLS. Clients MUST NOT offer these cipher suites if they do not offer TLS 1.2 or later, and servers that select an earlier version of TLS MUST NOT select one of these cipher suites. Because TLS has no way for the client to indicate that it supports TLS 1.2 but not earlier, a non-compliant server might potentially negotiate TLS 1.1 or earlier and select one of the cipher suites in this document. Clients MUST check the TLS version and generate a fatal illegal_parameter alert if they detect an incorrect version.
sections.plainLanguage: These suites need the AEAD support that arrived in TLS 1.2, so they cannot be used with older versions. A client must not offer them unless it also offers TLS 1.2 or later, and a server that picks an older version must not choose one of them. Because a client cannot say which versions it supports, it must check the version that was actually negotiated and abort with an illegal_parameter alert if it is too old.

sections.title: New AEAD Algorithms
sections.content:
Two AEAD algorithms are defined: AEAD_AES_128_CCM_8, value 18, and AEAD_AES_256_CCM_8, value 19.

The AEAD_AES_128_CCM_8 authenticated encryption algorithm is identical to the AEAD_AES_128_CCM algorithm, except that it uses 8 octets for authentication instead of the full 16 octets used by AEAD_AES_128_CCM. Its ciphertext consists of the ciphertext output of the CCM encryption operation concatenated with the 8-octet authentication tag output of that operation. Test cases are provided in the CCM specification. The input and output lengths are the same as those for AEAD_AES_128_CCM, and an AEAD_AES_128_CCM_8 ciphertext is exactly 8 octets longer than its corresponding plaintext.

The AEAD_AES_256_CCM_8 authenticated encryption algorithm is identical to the AEAD_AES_256_CCM algorithm, except that it uses 8 octets for authentication instead of the full 16 octets used by AEAD_AES_256_CCM. Its ciphertext consists of the ciphertext output of the CCM encryption operation concatenated with the 8-octet authentication tag output of that operation. The input and output lengths are as for AEAD_AES_128_CCM, and an AEAD_AES_128_CCM_8 ciphertext is exactly 8 octets longer than its corresponding plaintext.
sections.plainLanguage: Two new AEAD algorithm identifiers are added, values 18 and 19. They are the existing AES-128 and AES-256 CCM algorithms with the authentication tag cut from 16 octets to 8. Everything else, including the input and output lengths, stays the same, so the ciphertext ends up 8 octets longer than the plaintext.

sections.title: IANA Considerations
sections.content: IANA has assigned the values for the ciphersuites defined in Sections 3 and 4 from the TLS Cipher Suite registry, and the values of the AEAD algorithms defined in Section 6 from the AEAD Algorithms registry.
sections.plainLanguage: IANA has registered the sixteen cipher suite numbers and the two new AEAD algorithm numbers.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The perfect forward secrecy properties of RSA-based TLS ciphersuites are discussed in the security analysis of the TLS 1.2 specification, and it should be noted that only the ephemeral Diffie-Hellman-based ciphersuites are capable of providing perfect forward secrecy.

AES-CCM security requires that the counter is never reused. The IV construction in Section 3 is designed to prevent counter reuse.
sections.plainLanguage: Only the suites that use ephemeral Diffie-Hellman give forward secrecy, so the plain RSA suites do not. And AES-CCM is only safe if the counter never repeats, which is why the nonce construction is fixed the way it is.
